q: Where in the body are the parathyroid glands found?

pts.a: On the back of the thyroid gland, in the neck

right: On the back of the thyroid gland, in the neck
wrong: On top of each kidney
At the base of the brain
Inside the pancreas
why: The four tiny parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid gland, in the neck.

q: State the function of parathyroid hormone.

pts.a: It raises the level of calcium in the blood
accept: it raises calcium levels in the blood

right: It raises the level of calcium in the blood
wrong: It lowers the level of calcium in the blood
It controls the metabolic rate
It makes the kidneys save water
why: Parathyroid hormone raises the calcium level in the blood, for example by releasing calcium from the bones.

q: Name the hormone secreted by the parathyroid glands.

pts.a: Parathyroid hormone (PTH)

right: Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
wrong: Thyroxine
TSH
Insulin
why: The parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH). Thyroxine comes from the thyroid itself, and TSH from the pituitary.

q: Explain why the parathyroid glands are described as endocrine glands.

pts.a: They are ductless and secrete their hormone straight into the blood
accept: they secrete a hormone into the blood

right: They have no ducts and secrete their hormone into the blood
wrong: They are found in the neck
They are attached to the thyroid
They release calcium from the bones
why: Endocrine glands are ductless: the parathyroids secrete parathyroid hormone straight into the blood.

q: What is the function of TSH?

pts.a: It stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete thyroxine
accept: it makes the thyroid release thyroxine
it causes thyroxine to be secreted

right: It stimulates the thyroid gland to secrete thyroxine
wrong: It lowers the level of blood glucose
It makes the kidneys reabsorb more water
It makes the uterus contract at birth
why: TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone) from the pituitary stimulates the thyroid to secrete thyroxine. Its name is its job.

q: Give one function of the hormone oxytocin.

pts.a: It makes the uterus contract during birth
accept: contraction of the uterus in labour

pts.a: It makes the breasts release milk

right: It makes the uterus contract during birth
wrong: It makes the ovaries release an egg
It makes the kidneys save water
It thickens the lining of the uterus
why: Oxytocin from the pituitary makes the muscles of the uterus contract during birth, and makes the breasts release milk.

q: Name the endocrine gland that secretes both TSH and oxytocin.

pts.a: The pituitary gland
accept: the pituitary at the base of the brain

right: The pituitary gland
wrong: The thyroid gland
The ovaries
The pancreas
why: The pituitary, at the base of the brain, secretes FSH, LH, TSH, ADH and oxytocin. TSH acts on the thyroid; it isn't made there.

q: Name two hormones, other than ADH, that are secreted by the pituitary gland.

pts.a: FSH (follicle stimulating hormone)
LH (luteinising hormone)
TSH (thyroid stimulating hormone)
Oxytocin

right: FSH and TSH
wrong: Insulin and thyroxine
Oestrogen and FSH
Adrenaline and TSH
why: The pituitary secretes FSH, LH, TSH and oxytocin as well as ADH. Insulin, thyroxine, oestrogen and adrenaline come from other glands.

q: Why do some athletes misuse anabolic steroids?

pts.a: They build muscle mass and strength

right: They build muscle mass and strength
wrong: They make the heart beat more slowly
They lower blood glucose
They help the body to lose water
why: Anabolic steroids act like testosterone: they build muscle mass and strength, which is why they are banned in sport.

q: Give one harmful effect of misusing anabolic steroids.

pts.a: Liver damage
Heart disease or high blood pressure
Infertility
Aggression or mood swings

right: They can damage the liver
wrong: They make the bones stronger
They improve eyesight
They lower body temperature
why: Misused steroids can damage the liver and heart, raise blood pressure, cause infertility and bring on aggression.

q: Explain why some endurance athletes misuse the hormone EPO.

pts.a: It increases the number of red blood cells made
So more oxygen is carried to the muscles

right: It makes more red blood cells, so more oxygen reaches the muscles
wrong: It makes more white blood cells, so infections are fought off
It builds muscle, so the athlete is stronger
It lowers the heart rate, so less oxygen is needed
why: EPO makes the body produce more red blood cells, so the blood carries more oxygen to the muscles for respiration. It is banned and thickens the blood.

q: Give two reasons why hormones such as anabolic steroids and EPO are banned in sport.

pts.a: They give an unfair advantage (cheating)
accept: an unfair advantage over other athletes

pts.a: They can damage the athlete's health

right: They give an unfair advantage and can damage the athlete's health
wrong: They are too expensive and hard to buy
They make athletes slower and weaker
They are natural and cannot be detected
why: Performance-enhancing hormones are banned because using them is cheating, giving an unfair advantage, and because they can seriously harm health.

q: Give one use of hormones in agriculture.

pts.a: Growth hormones make livestock grow faster, giving more meat
accept: to make cows produce more milk

pts.a: Hormones to make animals breed at the same time
accept: to bring sheep into heat together

right: Growth hormones make cattle grow faster, giving more meat
wrong: Pesticides kill insects on crops
Antibiotics treat infections in calves
Vaccines protect sheep from disease
why: Farmers can use growth hormones for more meat or milk (banned in the EU), or hormones to bring animals into breeding condition together.

q: Give one reason why a farmer might use hormones to time when the animals in a flock breed.

pts.a: The young are all born together, so they are easier to look after
accept: all the young can be sold at the same time

right: The young are all born together, so they are easier to look after
wrong: To make the meat taste better
To stop the animals getting infections
To make the animals grow more wool
why: When the animals breed at the same time, the young are born together, so the farmer can plan, care for them and sell them as one group.

q: Give one concern about using growth hormones in livestock farming.

pts.a: Hormone residues in the meat or milk could affect the health of people who eat it
accept: it may harm the people who eat the meat

pts.a: It harms the welfare of the animals

right: Hormone residues in the meat could affect human health
wrong: It makes the meat cheaper to buy
It makes the animals grow too slowly
It uses too much fertiliser
why: Residues of the hormones could end up in the meat and milk people eat, and there are animal welfare concerns: the EU bans growth hormones in livestock.

q: After a meal, blood glucose rises. Describe how the body brings it back to normal.

pts.a: The pancreas secretes insulin into the blood
Insulin makes body cells take in glucose
The liver stores glucose as glycogen

right: The pancreas secretes insulin, so cells take in glucose
wrong: The pancreas secretes glucagon, so the liver releases glucose
The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline, so the heart speeds up
The kidneys remove glucose in the urine
why: The pancreas detects the rise and secretes insulin. Insulin makes body cells take in glucose and the liver store it as glycogen, so blood glucose falls.

q: Explain why the control of blood glucose by insulin is an example of negative feedback.

pts.a: The response reverses the change: insulin brings glucose back down to normal
accept: it brings glucose back to normal

pts.a: As glucose falls, less insulin is secreted (it switches itself off)
accept: insulin secretion falls as glucose falls

right: Insulin brings glucose back to normal, then less insulin is made
wrong: Insulin makes glucose keep rising, so more insulin is made
Glucose is stored in the pancreas until it is needed
Nerves tell the muscles to use up glucose
why: In negative feedback the response reverses the change: insulin lowers glucose back to normal, and as it falls, less insulin is secreted.

q: Which organ detects a rise in blood glucose and responds by secreting insulin?

pts.a: The pancreas (its islets of Langerhans)

right: The pancreas
wrong: The liver
The adrenal glands
The pituitary gland
why: The pancreas is both receptor and control centre here: its islets of Langerhans detect the rise in glucose and secrete insulin.

q: Give one way that insulin lowers the level of glucose in the blood.

pts.a: Body cells (e.g. muscle cells) take in more glucose
The liver converts glucose to glycogen and stores it

right: It makes body cells take in glucose
wrong: It makes the kidneys excrete glucose
It makes the liver release more glucose
It stops food being digested
why: Insulin makes body cells, especially muscle and liver cells, take in glucose, and the liver stores it as glycogen.

q: In homeostasis, what is the job of a receptor?

pts.a: It detects a change (a stimulus)
accept: it notices a change in conditions

right: It detects a change in conditions
wrong: It carries out the response
It decides what response to make
It carries the hormone in the blood
why: Receptors detect the change (the stimulus); the control centre decides on the response; effectors carry it out, through nerves or hormones.

q: In the control of blood glucose, name an effector that carries out the response to insulin.

pts.a: The liver (or muscle cells)

right: The liver
wrong: The pituitary gland
The kidneys
The thyroid gland
why: The liver and muscle cells are the effectors: they take in glucose, and the liver stores it as glycogen.

q: Explain what is meant by negative feedback in homeostasis.

pts.a: A change causes a response that reverses it, bringing conditions back to normal
accept: it brings conditions back to normal
the response cancels out the change

right: A change causes a response that reverses it, back to normal
wrong: A change causes a response that makes it bigger
The body ignores small changes
Hormones are broken down after they are used
why: In negative feedback the response reverses the change, bringing conditions back to normal; a response that makes the change bigger is positive feedback.

q: Name the two pathways that can link a control centre to its effectors in homeostasis.

pts.a: The nervous pathway (nerves)
The hormonal pathway (hormones)

right: Nerves and hormones
wrong: Blood vessels and lymph
Muscles and bones
Nerves and enzymes
why: Homeostasis uses nervous and hormonal pathways to link the control centre with receptors and effectors.
